reasons.i-start: At the start of a word, an i before a vowel is a consonant, like English y: iam = jam.
reasons.i-between: Between two vowels, i is a consonant, and it counts twice: Troia = Troj-ja.
reasons.i-prefix: After a prefix (con-, ad-, sub-, ob-, in-, dis-), an i before u, a or -ec- is a consonant: con-jūnx, sub-jec-ta.
reasons.i-final: After a consonant, i is a vowel, its own syllable -- and so at the end of a word: om-ni-a, nes-ci-o.
reasons.i-after: After a consonant inside a word, i is a vowel, its own syllable: fī-li-us.
reasons.i-eo: The i of eō, “go” (īre, iit), stays a vowel after a prefix: ab-i-it, co-i-ē-re.
reasons.i-name: A few names begin with a vowel i: I-ā-sōn, I-ū-lus.
reasons.d-common: ae, au and oe are diphthongs: one syllable, and long.
reasons.d-rare: ei, eu and ui are diphthongs only in a few words: heu, seu, neu, cui, huic, dein(de), and Greek names like Orpheus.
reasons.a-lookalike: Outside those few words, e-u, e-i and u-i stay apart: de-us, me-us, fu-it.
reasons.a-split: A macron, or a prefix, splits them: ā-ēr, co-er-cet, Trō-es.
reasons.a-ai: ai is never a diphthong in Latin: a-it.
reasons.a-other: These two vowels are no diphthong, so each is its own syllable: me-a, tu-ō.
